mcqs.question: Why should an order's cancellation options shrink as it moves through PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, and PICKED_UP?
options: Allowing cancellation at every stage, including after pickup, matches real-world constraints once food has physically left the restaurant
Cancellation should be identical at every stage for simplicity
Cancellation after pickup means food is already out for delivery and can't reasonably be un-cooked or un-dispatched, so the design should reflect that a cancel path no longer makes sense
The state machine has no bearing on which actions should be permitted
mcqs.explanation: Once food is picked up, cancellation isn't practically meaningful — the state machine should encode that instead of allowing a cancel action everywhere. Uniform cancellation everywhere ignores physical reality, and the state machine is precisely what should govern allowed actions.

mcqs.question: What's the downside of assigning a delivery partner the instant an order is placed, before the restaurant starts preparing it?
options: The order can never be cancelled after that point
The delivery partner may sit idle at the restaurant if prep takes longer than expected, wasting their time and reducing availability for other orders
The restaurant is not allowed to reject the order anymore
The customer's payment is charged twice
mcqs.explanation: Early assignment risks partner idle time if the kitchen is backed up. It doesn't block cancellation, doesn't prevent restaurant rejection, and has nothing to do with double-charging.

mcqs.question: What should determine whether a restaurant assigns delivery partners early (at order-time) or late (at pickup-ready-time)?
options: How predictable that restaurant's prep time is — predictable kitchens can safely assign early, volatile ones should assign closer to actual readiness
The restaurant's cuisine type has no bearing on this decision, it should always be a fixed global policy
The customer's delivery address distance, regardless of prep-time predictability
mcqs.explanation: Prep-time predictability is what actually drives the trade-off between partner idle time and delivery latency. A single global policy ignores real variance between restaurants, and payment fees and delivery distance aren't the deciding factors here.

mcqs.question: What's the problem with putting acceptByRestaurant(), assignPartner(), and processPayment() all as methods directly on the Order class?
options: Order objects would use too much memory to be practical
Java and similar languages technically forbid more than two public methods per class
It would make Order impossible to serialize to JSON
Order becomes a god object that changes for reasons owned by three different concerns, so a change to one risks breaking the others
mcqs.explanation: Concentrating unrelated responsibilities in one class means unrelated changes collide there — the actual single-responsibility problem. Memory, serialization, and language method-count limits aren't real constraints here.
